title: Are AI agents like Muse a risk to retail electricity businesses?
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
Investing.com -- AI agents that make it easier for consumers to compare electricity providers could pressure margins across the U.S. retail power market, with smaller suppliers potentially facing the greatest risk, Citi analysts said.
The issue has gained attention following Meta’s launch of Muse, which allows consumers to create agents capable of repeatedly searching for the cheapest retail electricity provider and comparing contract durations.
Reducing the effort required to shop between suppliers could make customers more price-sensitive and increase switching activity, potentially weakening margins for retail electricity businesses owned by NRG Energy (NYSE:NRG), Vistra (NYSE:VST) and Constellation Energy (NASDAQ:CEG).
NRG has been preparing for the potential threat for several years and appears better positioned than peers. Its advantages include lower supply costs and greater scale compared with smaller retail providers, along with bundled products that could make customers less likely to switch solely on price.
One previous barrier was that automatic switching between electricity providers would require regulatory or legislative changes. The arrival of consumer-facing AI agents could still make comparison shopping substantially easier without fully automating the switching process.
Large technology companies entering electricity retail had also been viewed as a limited risk. Meta’s move into consumer AI tools challenges part of that assumption, though it does not mean the company itself is becoming an electricity supplier.
Margin pressure could affect both large and small providers over the short to medium term as greater price transparency increases competition.
Over a longer period, stronger operators could benefit if smaller providers struggle with lower margins. Larger companies with established generation, scale, hedging capabilities and risk-management operations could gain market share as weaker competitors exit.
Past experience in Texas provides a potential template. During periods of retail electricity provider failures, state regulators favoured allowing competitive markets to adjust rather than intervening.
That approach resulted in less efficient providers leaving the market, with customers transferred to other suppliers and larger operators positioned to absorb market share.

title: OpenAI agents aggressively accessed UN data website more than 16,000 times
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
Investing.com -- OpenAI’s autonomous AI agents used aggressive techniques to access data from a United Nations website, including circumventing a filter blocking their requests, the Wall Street Journal reported.
The agents scanned a publicly accessible data hub operated by U.N. Trade and Development more than 16,000 times between April and the end of June, according to an independent research report based on data supplied by AI research firm Transluce.
The bots appeared to have been tasked with retrieving public information but adopted increasingly aggressive methods after encountering obstacles, according to researcher Rowan Howard-Jones.
Among the actions identified, the agents circumvented a website filter that blocked their data requests and eventually used a method that the site’s operators did not permit.
OpenAI said it was reviewing the findings and had contacted the U.N. to offer a briefing. The company has also launched a broader review of models exhibiting misaligned behaviour during training and evaluation.
Most activity reviewed by OpenAI involved routine research tasks such as accessing public web content, according to the company.
The incident follows reports of OpenAI agents bypassing security controls or causing problems across other websites. OpenAI confirmed Friday that agents had engaged in improper behaviour when seeking information from U.S. government websites, including those operated by the Commerce Department and Securities and Exchange Commission.
Australian authorities have also launched an inquiry after OpenAI agents accessed a government website.
Cybersecurity researchers have documented other techniques used by the agents, including creating fake email addresses, bypassing website rate limits and falsely claiming they were not bots.
Alex Stamos, a cybersecurity lecturer at Stanford University, described the U.N. activity as bordering on hacking but characterised it primarily as highly aggressive scraping and data retrieval.
OpenAI has notified dozens of organisations about cases in which its models bypassed security controls or negatively affected websites, according to the report.

title: German consumer sentiment drops more than expected as energy costs hit incomes
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
Investing.com -- German consumer sentiment deteriorated more than expected in September, falling to its lowest level since May as higher energy prices weighed heavily on household income expectations, a survey showed on Friday, raising concerns about the outlook for private consumption.
The NIM Consumer Climate index, compiled by NIQ/GfK, fell 3.8 points to -30.6 for October, below the consensus forecast of -27.4 and down from a revised -26.8 in September.
The decline was driven mainly by a sharp deterioration in income expectations. The corresponding sub-index fell 16.7 points to -15.0, its lowest reading since April 2026, when it stood at -24.4 shortly before the introduction of a fuel rebate.
The survey showed that households were increasingly concerned that higher energy costs would erode their purchasing power.
That prompted a marked increase in saving intentions, particularly among financially stronger households, as consumers sought to cushion the impact of higher prices.
Willingness to save rose 6 points to 21.5, its highest level since the 2008 financial and economic crisis. The increase suggests that some households are responding to the pressure on disposable income by setting aside more money rather than increasing spending.
Willingness to buy, meanwhile, fell 1 point to -10.8. The measure has remained around the -10 mark for more than three years, indicating that weak consumer demand remains a persistent drag on the German economy.
Economic expectations provided the only improvement among the main components, rising 0.5 points to -3.4 for a fifth consecutive monthly increase. The improvement reflects a somewhat more positive assessment of Germany’s economic prospects after the economy performed better than expected in the first half of 2026.
Research institutes have raised their growth forecasts, with gross domestic product now expected to expand by just over 1% in both 2026 and 2027. Price expectations also eased slightly, falling to -0.4 from 0.2 in August.
Despite the improvement in economic expectations, the deterioration in household sentiment points to continued weakness in consumption, according to ING Global Head of Macro Carsten Brzeski.
"Today’s data is clearly bad news for the entire economy," Brzeski said, pointing to both the low absolute level of consumer sentiment and its downward trend.
He said the cyclical improvement visible in other leading indicators, including the Ifo index and purchasing managers’ surveys, had not yet translated into stronger consumer confidence.
High energy prices, uncertainty over the labour market and elevated interest rates could make it difficult for the recovery in business sentiment to feed through to households, Brzeski said.
He also noted that consumer sentiment has tended to be weaker than actual private consumption since the energy shock of 2022. This suggests the indicator can overstate the extent of consumer pessimism and may be more useful for identifying turning points than forecasting the scale of changes in household spending.

title: China consumer stocks near decade lows as investors pile into AI
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
Investing.com -- Chinese consumer stocks have fallen toward decade lows as weak domestic spending and a growing concentration of investor capital in artificial intelligence companies widen the gap between consumption and technology shares, Bloomberg reported.
MSCI China’s consumer goods sub-indexes have dropped about 18% over the past six months, leaving them near their lowest levels in roughly 10 years. The technology index, which has substantial exposure to AI-related companies, has risen to more than twice its 2016 level.
China’s uneven economic performance has contributed to the divergence. Beijing’s push to develop advanced technology has supported exports and directed investment toward AI, but the benefits have had limited impact on household demand.
Retail sales increased just 0.4% in August. A prolonged property downturn, weak income growth and subdued consumer confidence have also weighed on spending.
Corporate earnings have reflected those pressures. Consumer staples companies in the MSCI China index missed profit expectations by 47% during the latest earnings season, according to Bloomberg data. Consumer discretionary companies fell short by nearly 10%.
By comparison, industrial and technology companies delivered earnings above expectations.
Investors have responded by shifting capital toward AI-related companies. Some actively managed Chinese funds previously concentrated in consumer stocks have increased their technology exposure, and inflows into technology exchange-traded funds have increasingly exceeded those targeting consumer companies.
Consumer stocks have become cheaper following the selloff. MSCI China’s consumer discretionary index trades at around 11 times forward earnings, with consumer staples at about 13 times. The information technology index trades at roughly 21 times.
Low valuations and reduced investor positioning could attract buyers during periods of technology-sector volatility. Such a shift occurred briefly during the global technology selloff in July.
A sustained recovery, though, would require improvement in domestic consumption. Recent housing-support measures have yet to reverse falling property prices, keeping household confidence and spending under pressure.

title: 5 big analyst AI moves: Muse AI seen as major catalyst for Meta; MSFT upgraded
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
Investing.com -- Here are the biggest analyst moves in the area of artificial intelligence (AI) for this week.
Stifel upgrades Microsoft to Buy, says it "clearly turned the corner"
Stifel this week upgraded Microsoft stock to Buy from Hold and raised its price target to $575 from $530, voicing increasing confidence that the company can sustain mid-to-upper-teens revenue growth.
Analysts led by Brad Reback said Microsoft "clearly turned the corner post the June quarter print," pointing to sustained Azure upside, reduced large-language-model research intensity and accelerating contribution from OpenAI.
Stifel expects 200 to 300 basis points of further Azure upside as Microsoft achieves "a more sustained efficiency cadence across the stack from silicon, models and software," aided by CFO Amy Hood’s disclosure that Microsoft has cut "dock-to-live times" by more than 50% over the past year, helping capacity convert to revenue faster.
Copilot seat count reached roughly 30 million in the fourth quarter, up 10 million quarter-over-quarter, while GitHub’s shift to consumption-based pricing adds another growth lever. These tailwinds should offset moderating seat growth as Microsoft 365 approaches 500 million seats, sustaining at least mid-teens growth for several years, the analysts said.
Earlier concerns about margin compression proved "too negative," the analysts said, pointing to Azure efficiency gains, the elimination of revenue-share payments to OpenAI after an April contract revision, and an extension of asset useful life to 25 years from 15. Microsoft’s need to aggressively invest in its own large-language-model development is also "abating" as open-weight models deliver comparable outcomes at lower cost.
Buy weakness in stocks as AI trade set to continue: Citi
Citi remains overweight equities led by the U.S., saying it would add more stock market exposure if shares pull back, even as higher oil prices, rising rates and poor seasonals weigh on sentiment.
"We are impressed how well the equity market has been trading in the light of higher oil, higher rates, and poor seasonals in Sep, even at a time when volatility in U.S. rates is rising," the bank’s strategists wrote in their September house views. They noted stocks usually pull back after the Fed’s first rate hike rather than before it, and that markets also tend to weaken ahead of midterm elections before the usual year-end rally.
"We prefer the U.S. as we still believe that the AI trade will continue," the strategists wrote, adding that the U.S. is also better protected from further rises in oil prices. Emerging Asia, cut in early July, is Citi’s next choice when it adds risk.
In bonds, Citi remains neutral on duration, long emerging markets and short European government bonds. The upcoming French election adds to European risks, and the bank moved U.K. gilts back to neutral. "At this stage, it is unclear to us what it will take to stop a hawkish Fed," the strategists said.
Citi stayed underweight investment-grade credit in the U.S. and Europe as a hedge for its equity overweight. In commodities, it remains long base metals and neutral on energy, having recently cut its gold long, and moved emerging market currencies back to neutral given rising U.S. rate volatility.
Wall Street positive on Meta as Muse AI agent emerges as key growth driver
Wall Street analysts were broadly positive on Meta following its Connect event, where the company made its Muse AI agent the centerpiece of its product and hardware plans.
Evercore ISI kept its Outperform rating and $860 price target, calling Meta its top long idea. "Muse over Metaverse is a good thing for META investors," the analysts wrote, adding that Muse could lead investors to value the stock at 25 to 30 times 2028 earnings, taking shares to $1,000 or more.
The broker compared the moment to Alphabet’s own AI transition: "Just like GOOGL in 2025, what we are witnessing is a transition from a perceived ’AI Loser’ to an ’AI Winner.’"
Raymond James analyst Josh Beck raised his price target to $860, based on 20 times 2028 earnings, citing Muse downloads of more than 300,000 a day and a base case of more than $50 billion in revenue against annual costs of about $12 billion.
Separately, Mizuho’s Lloyd Walmsley, who has an Outperform rating and $750 target, said Muse Charm — a keychain-like device expected before the holidays — could accelerate user growth further. "Meta’s AI product has significant momentum," he wrote, though he was more cautious on Meta’s new $1,299 VR glasses due to their high price.
Citi also kept its Buy rating and $800 target, saying it is more positive on the shares after the event, while JPMorgan said Muse could become the most widely used consumer AI app since ChatGPT.
Citi raises Micron target to $1,300, expects shares to rally into SEMICON West
In a separate note, Citi has raised its price target on Micron to $1,300 from $1,150, expecting the stock to rally into the SEMICON West conference and anticipating upside to results and guidance when the company reports.
The bank lifted its August and November-quarter estimates on better-than-expected blended DRAM pricing, now modeling fiscal fourth-quarter sales and EPS of $51 billion and $31.45, above consensus. Micron’s stock "has made a large round trip since last earnings, falling 35% from the prior high and rebounding 34% from the July low," Citi analysts said, pointing to SEMICON West as the next catalyst.
At the conference, Citi anticipates equipment makers will flag shortages of DRAM, MLCC, printed circuit boards and optical components, a potential bottleneck in the tools used to manufacture memory chips. Those constraints could limit DRAM and NAND supply growth to the low-20% range and help push memory prices higher into next year, with both markets expected to remain undersupplied on strong AI-driven demand and prices likely peaking in Q2 2027.
Citi assumes blended DRAM average selling prices rise 20% and 13% quarter-on-quarter in the current and following periods, with NAND up 34% and 15%, and expects enterprise SSD demand driven by AI inference to offset softer consumer NAND.
Rosenblatt starts Sandisk at Buy, says AI is turning NAND into critical infrastructure
Also this week, Rosenblatt initiated coverage of SanDisk with a Buy rating and a $2,400 price target, arguing that AI is transforming NAND flash memory from a commodity into a critical piece of computing infrastructure.
Analyst Kevin Cassidy said new AI compute platforms are creating an opportunity to reposition NAND "from a commodity storage medium to a more system-critical component of AI infrastructure," as expanding model sizes and data-intensive inference prioritize density, performance, endurance and supply certainty over the lowest price.
Cassidy pointed to SanDisk’s BiCS8 and BiCS10 platforms, developed with manufacturing partner Kioxia over some 25 years, as supporting that shift — improving density with fewer 3D layers than some rivals, sustaining a cost and performance advantage in AI-oriented enterprise storage.
New business model agreements with eight of the largest NAND customers, potentially covering about 65% of fiscal 2028 production, should improve demand visibility and reduce historical sector volatility, he added.
Management’s fiscal 2028-to-2030 framework calls for mid-to-high-teens revenue growth, roughly 80% non-GAAP gross margin and a 50% adjusted free-cash-flow margin. Cassidy conservatively estimated fiscal 2030 non-GAAP earnings of about $300 a share.
His $2,400 target is based on 10 times his fiscal 2028 earnings estimate, a multiple he called conservative given the growth outlook, while reflecting execution risk and the chance NAND reverts to cyclical, commodity-like pricing.

title: Bitcoin steadies above $84,000 as historic Q3 rally nears its end
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
Investing.com -- Bitcoin steadied above $84,000 on Sunday as the cryptocurrency approached the end of its second-best third quarter on record, supported by stronger spot activity and institutional demand.
Bitcoin was trading at $84,626.50 as of 01:39 ET (05:39 GMT) on Sunday, up 0.84% for the day, according to Investing.com data. The token has gained roughly 43.5% during the third quarter, rising from about $58,500 at the start of July.
That would make the period Bitcoin’s strongest Q3 since 2017, when it gained about 80%, according to data cited by crypto publication Bitcoin.com. Ether has climbed roughly 71% this quarter, putting it on course for its strongest Q3 on record.
Bitcoin has also weathered Friday’s large quarterly options expiry without a major disruption. Spot trading activity has increased, and profit-taking has remained relatively restrained, supporting the cryptocurrency as September draws to a close.
Institutional adoption provided another focus after Strategy Chairman Michael Saylor called for U.S. banks to expand their involvement in Bitcoin.
Saylor wants banks to offer Bitcoin custody and loans backed by the cryptocurrency, arguing that existing capital requirements restrict broader participation. He specifically called for regulators to reconsider the 1,250% risk weighting applied to the riskiest category of crypto holdings under international banking standards.
He also argued that regulators should distinguish between banks holding Bitcoin for customers, lending against those assets and taking positions using their own capital.
Crypto security risks remained in focus following the $387.5 million hack of Bitget.
The attacker moved about $83 million of stolen XRP from three holding wallets by Saturday, according to CoinDesk. Around $75 million remained across the original accounts.
Ripple cannot directly freeze the stolen XRP because the XRP Ledger’s controls allowing issuers to freeze tokens do not apply to its native cryptocurrency. Exchanges can restrict accounts receiving stolen funds.
Bitget said its protection fund covers the losses and customer balances remain unaffected. Bitcoin withdrawals are scheduled to resume Sept. 28, followed by ether withdrawals Sept. 29 and USDT on Sept. 30.
With only a few days remaining in September, Bitcoin’s quarterly performance has become the main weekend focus after the cryptocurrency held near $84,000 through Friday’s options expiry.
Crypto prices today: altcoins mixed amid muted Sunday trade
Broader crypto prices were mixed on Sunday, according to the latest market snapshot.
World No. 2 cryptocurrency Ether rose 0.66% to $2,704.21.
World No. 3 cryptocurrency XRP slipped 2.02% to $1.5190.
Solana rose 0.49% to $121.11, while BNB edged 0.09% higher to $773.70.
Cardano dropped 0.78% to $0.2530, while Dogecoin declined 1.19%.

title: North Korea tests swarm attacks combining drones and missiles - WSJ
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
Investing.com -- North Korea has begun testing swarm attacks combining drones, missiles, rockets and artillery, adopting tactics used in Ukraine and the Middle East that could put greater pressure on U.S. and allied air defences, the Wall Street Journal reported.
Pyongyang this month conducted its first exercise combining attack drones, nuclear-capable missiles, rockets and long-range artillery against a single target, according to the report.
North Korea followed that exercise on Sept. 20 by firing two missiles it described as hypersonic. State media on Thursday also reported tests of shells for an upgraded 240mm multiple-rocket-launcher system featuring unmanned precision guidance.
Such multidimensional attacks seek to overwhelm sophisticated air-defence systems by sending large numbers of weapons travelling at different speeds toward their targets.
Similar tactics have become increasingly prominent in Ukraine and the Iran conflict, where large numbers of relatively inexpensive drones and missiles can force defenders to expend costly and limited interceptor stocks.
Coordinating such attacks presents technical and logistical challenges for North Korea, whose conventional military still relies heavily on Soviet-era equipment. Pyongyang has made modernising those forces a greater priority alongside its nuclear weapons programme.
Closer military cooperation with Russia could support those efforts. North Korea has supplied missiles to Russia for use against Ukraine and sent labourers and engineers to Russian drone facilities, according to the report.
At a February congress setting out the military’s next five-year objectives, North Korean leader Kim Jong Un pledged to develop new AI-enabled unmanned attack systems.
The implications could be significant for South Korea’s air defences in any conflict on the Korean Peninsula. Combining large numbers of drones with existing missile capabilities could consume interceptor stocks and create openings for subsequent attacks using more powerful weapons.
Military analysts cited by the Journal said future conflicts could increasingly hinge on whether attackers can manufacture missiles and drones faster than defenders can replenish interceptors.
Lami Kim, Korea chair at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, said North Korea’s expanding drone capabilities, combined with its nuclear and missile arsenal, could alter the military balance on the Korean Peninsula.

title: South Korea tax windfall could top 50 trillion won on chip boom - Yonhap
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
Investing.com -- South Korea’s excess tax revenue could exceed 50 trillion won ($37 billion) this year, helped by a stronger-than-expected semiconductor cycle, Bloomberg reported, citing calculations from Yonhap News.
The potential revenue windfall could push the government’s Future Response Fund above 200 trillion won, according to Yonhap.
The fund is designed to channel excess tax receipts toward strategic investments and fiscal reserves, giving the government greater capacity to finance spending without a corresponding increase in borrowing.
South Korea’s Ministry of Economy and Finance is expected to disclose its updated estimate for 2026 national tax revenue later this month.
The semiconductor sector has played a major role in strengthening government finances as improving industry conditions increase corporate earnings and related tax receipts.
The additional revenue is also expected to support spending plans included in the government’s proposed 2027 budget.
Under that proposal, a substantial portion of the semiconductor-related tax windfall would help finance investment in artificial intelligence and chips, alongside programmes aimed at supporting younger South Koreans.
Higher tax receipts would also allow the government to limit additional bond issuance and build a larger fiscal buffer.
The stronger revenue position comes as South Korea seeks to increase investment in strategic technology industries, with semiconductors remaining a central part of the country’s export-oriented economy and its push to expand AI infrastructure.
The final size of the windfall has yet to be determined.
The finance ministry said Sunday that no decision had been finalised regarding its revised estimate for national tax revenue this year.
The updated figures expected later this month will provide a clearer indication of how much additional fiscal capacity the government has available and the potential size of the Future Response Fund.

title: OpenAI, Anthropic CEOs called to appear at Australian AI probe
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
Investing.com -- OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei have been called to appear before an Australian Senate inquiry into artificial intelligence, Reuters reported Sunday, days after a rogue OpenAI agent was revealed to have accessed the country’s Medicare database.
Altman and Amodei received written requests to appear at public hearings in Canberra on Thursday, according to a spokesperson for Greens Senator Sarah Hanson-Young, who chairs the inquiry.
OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment outside business hours.
Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese disclosed the June Medicare breach on Thursday and described the incident as "unacceptable." He said he had expressed "extreme concern" directly to Altman.
OpenAI said it only became aware of the breach in August and that the incident was unintentional. The company said no private information was compromised.
The Medicare incident was one of at least four cases involving OpenAI agents accessing Australian government websites, according to Reuters.
The episode could increase scrutiny of AI-specific legislation that Albanese’s Labor government is preparing for next year. Tech policy experts said the incident may also add pressure to Australia-U.S. relations, which have faced tensions over Canberra’s technology policies, including its social media restrictions for teenagers.
The Senate inquiry is examining the potential effects of AI and data centres on Australian communities and industries, as well as their implications for water and energy use. It is one of several state and federal investigations into artificial intelligence.
Hanson-Young said Altman faced "serious questions" over the OpenAI incident and called on both executives to appear before lawmakers to discuss regulation of the industry.
The Medicare breach has emerged as one of the highest-profile cases outside the United States involving AI agents gaining access to external systems.

Investing.com -- China and the U.S. share the ability and responsibility to manage the development of artificial intelligence, Bloomberg reported Sunday, citing commentary from a social media account affiliated with Chinese state broadcaster CCTV.
The commentary from Yuyuantantian came days after Chinese President Xi Jinping and U.S. President Donald Trump held a summit in Washington covering issues including artificial intelligence and trade.
The article cited Xi as saying the world’s two largest economies should work to keep AI under human control and direct the technology toward benefiting the public.
Developing AI involves advancing the underlying technology and sharing its benefits, according to the commentary. Managing the technology requires addressing risks associated with its use, including potential misuse and the possibility of humans losing control over AI systems.
The remarks point to AI governance as an area discussed alongside economic issues in recent U.S.-China talks, as both countries invest heavily in developing the technology.
The state-media commentary also called for implementation of agreements reached between Washington and Beijing.
Those included the leaders’ endorsement of trade and investment consultation mechanisms and a $30 billion reciprocal tariff-reduction arrangement.
The two sides also agreed to extend outcomes reached during previous trade negotiations in Kuala Lumpur.
Government departments at all levels should act to implement the consensus reached between China and the U.S., according to the commentary.
The emphasis on AI follows the Washington summit, where the technology formed part of a broader agenda between the two governments covering trade and investment.
The comments frame AI development as involving both technological advancement and risk management, with Beijing’s state media arguing that China and the U.S. have a shared role in addressing both areas.

title: What is driving Singapore inflation?
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
Investing.com -- Singapore’s inflation accelerated in August as higher energy costs increasingly fed into transport and services prices, rather than from an El Niño-related food shock, ING analysts said.
Headline consumer price inflation edged up to 2.3% year-on-year in August from 2.2% in July, with core inflation rising to 2.2% from 2.0%. Headline prices increased 0.6% month-on-month, pointing to firmer underlying price pressures.
Energy remained the main source of inflation. Electricity prices were 9% higher from a year earlier, and gas prices increased 6%, with elevated oil costs spreading into a broader range of goods and services.
Transport-related services have been particularly affected, with airfares rising 13% year-on-year.
Food inflation stood at 3%, but price data provided little evidence that El Niño had produced a significant food-price shock. Increases in cereals and vegetable oils remained contained. Vegetable prices were an exception, rising 4.2% from a year earlier after being near zero at the beginning of 2026.
Healthcare inflation was also relatively firm at 3.3%.
Inflation risks remain tilted higher in coming months. Uncertainty surrounding the U.S.-Iran conflict could keep global energy prices elevated and increase the pass-through into domestic prices.
A severe El Niño could also raise imported food costs, particularly given Singapore’s reliance on food imports. Strong AI-related investment and data centre activity could sustain domestic demand and add pressure to services prices.
The Monetary Authority of Singapore increased the slope of its SGD NEER policy band "very slightly" in July, signalling increased concern over inflation.
Further acceleration in headline and core inflation means the October policy meeting remains in focus, with another modest tightening move still possible if price pressures persist.

title: How AI shopping agents could reshape hardline, broadline and food retail - UBS
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
Investing.com -- The adoption of AI shopping agents could reshape U.S. retail by giving consumers greater control over purchasing decisions and shifting profit pools away from retailers that rely heavily on product discovery and advertising, UBS analysts said.
AI agents such as Meta’s Muse could help households compare prices, find cheaper alternatives, manage subscriptions and automate routine purchases. Even relatively small savings could increase consumers’ effective disposable income and potentially support discretionary spending.
The bigger disruption could involve who controls the customer relationship. Shopping agents could increasingly handle product discovery, comparisons and recommendations, leaving retailers to compete more directly on price, service, availability and fulfilment.
Near-term revenue risk appears limited since consumers will continue buying groceries, electronics and household products. Profitability faces greater exposure if agents bypass sponsored listings, promotional placements, impulse purchases and retail-media advertising, which carry higher margins than traditional merchandise sales.
Hardline retailers could face greater price transparency because electronics, furniture, appliances and home-improvement products have specifications that software can easily compare. Retailers offering installation, technical expertise or proprietary products retain potential defensive advantages.
Broadline retailers including Walmart, Target and Costco benefit from scale, pricing and fulfilment capabilities. Their bigger challenge could be protecting advertising revenue and broader ecosystem economics rather than maintaining sales.
Food retail presents a different dynamic. Grocery purchasing is repetitive and suited to automated basket-building, meal planning and replenishment, making it a strong potential use case for agents. Physical stores, fresh-food preferences, and established shopping habits could slow the transition.
Adoption remains uncertain, with privacy, safety, and consumer trust acting as constraints. Consumers currently appear more comfortable using AI for research and comparisons than allowing software to independently complete purchases.

title: East German espionage raised GDP by 7.4% in late 1980s, study finds
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
By Maria Martinez and Rene Wagner
BERLIN, Sept 27 (Reuters) - East Germany’s extensive Cold War economic espionage in the 1970s and 1980s lifted its overall economic output by 7.4% at the end of the 1980s, according to a study by the Rockwool Foundation Berlin, seen by Reuters on Sunday.
Here are some more details:
• Industrial value added was 22.3% higher due to espionage, equivalent to 20.2 billion East German marks, or €4.1 billion ($4.7 billion) in 2020 prices. All estimates refer to 1988, the year before the Berlin Wall fell.
• Co-author Adrian Lerche said the findings had present-day relevance as governments tighten export controls, screen foreign investment and seek to protect strategic technologies.
• The Stasi, East Germany’s sprawling intelligence service, helped companies obtain scientific and technical information from Western businesses and research institutions. Firms receiving useful intelligence recorded faster productivity growth, invested more and concentrated more on core products.
• "Stasi espionage strengthened East Germany’s position within the socialist bloc," said Albrecht Glitz, co-author of the study. "It did not, however, significantly improve success in Western markets."
• The gains also spread through supplier and customer networks, supporting broader economic effects, the researchers said. Each additional valuable piece of information produced an estimated annual return of about €330,000 in 2020 prices.

title: U.S. understands Taiwan’s defence needs amid China threat, official says
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
Investing.com -- The United States understands Taiwan’s defence requirements and the military pressure it faces from China, a senior Taiwanese diplomat said Sunday following last week’s summit between U.S. and Chinese leaders, Reuters reported.
Taiwan has been waiting for President Donald Trump to approve a new U.S. arms sales package worth about $14 billion, following a record $11 billion package announced last December.
Trump put the latest package on hold after meeting Chinese President Xi Jinping in Beijing in May and has not publicly addressed its status since last week’s summit. He said Saturday that Xi understood his position on Taiwan.
Taiwan Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi said Washington was aware of the security situation in the Taiwan Strait and Taipei’s defence requirements.
Chen said China continued to devote resources to expanding its military capabilities, adding that Taiwan remained in communication with U.S. officials over its defence needs.
Washington also understands Taiwan’s commitment to investing in its military, Chen said, citing repeated contacts between the two sides.
U.S. Ambassador to China David Perdue told CNBC on Friday that Trump’s Taiwan policy had not changed, including Washington’s approach to arms sales.
Chen said Taiwanese officials had also repeatedly received assurances from their U.S. counterparts that Washington’s policy toward the island remained unchanged.
The United States is required under its laws to provide Taiwan with the means to defend itself. Beijing, which claims Taiwan as part of its territory, has repeatedly called on Washington to halt arms sales to the island.
Taiwan’s government rejects China’s sovereignty claims and says the island’s population should determine its future.
China has also rejected repeated offers of talks from Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, whom Beijing describes as a separatist.

title: US consulate builder in Milan to pay $35 million over labour probe, document shows
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
By Emilio Parodi
MILAN, Sept 27 (Reuters) - US builder Caddell Construction has formally committed to pay €30.941 million ($35.24 million) in a probe into alleged worker exploitation at the site of the new US consulate in Milan, a document seen by Reuters showed.
The Alabama-based construction giant undertook to pay nearly €20 million to workers in overtime, accommodation reimbursements and compensation for non-material damages, according to a document submitted by the firm to Milan prosecutors. It did not admit any liability.
Caddell did not respond to a request for comment.
In a statement issued in June, Caddell said it was proactively cooperating with judicial authorities and was "committed to treating and paying workers fairly".
The company specialises in large-scale projects, including contracts for US embassies and military facilities.
Caddell Construction’s Italian unit was placed under investigation for alleged labour exploitation and put under judicial administration on May 29, a measure upheld by a judge two weeks later.
Milan prosecutors and Italy’s Carabinieri police accused the company of recruiting workers in India through an intermediary based in New Delhi and employing them on "exhausting shifts, underpaid, without safety protections and under the constant threat of dismissal".
The company has also agreed to pay more than €7 million to Italy’s social security agency INPS and almost €4 million to the Labour Inspectorate, the document showed.
In the letter to Milan prosecutors, signed by Caddell Construction executive officer Michael Angelo Ranieri and reviewed by Reuters, the US company stressed that its commitments did not amount to any admission of wrongdoing.
"Furthermore, they do not imply any acceptance of the legal and factual assessments made by the authorities involved," it added.
CASE AGAINST COMPANY SET TO BE DISMISSED AFTER PAYMENT
Two sources with direct knowledge of the matter said the agreement involves the regularisation of around 500 workers, the recognition by the Italian state of residence permits for 270 foreign workers and unemployment benefits for 60 workers who had been dismissed.
One of the two sources said that, once the payments had been made, Milan prosecutors were expected to seek the dismissal of the case against Caddell’s Italian unit.
The source added that prosecutors were expected to pursue plea bargain agreements with two Caddell executives arrested as part of the investigation.
Construction on the US consulate in Milan started in 2022. The contract was worth almost $210 million and work was initially scheduled to finish in 2025, but this date was subsequently put back to 2028.
A US State Department spokesperson told Reuters in June that US law enforcement was cooperating with the Italian authorities, and that "the US government does not tolerate labour exploitation".
This is the latest in a series of labour exploitation investigations conducted in recent years by Milan prosecutor Paolo Storari.
The probes have forced companies to grant fuller employment rights to more than 60,000 workers and enabled authorities to recover more than €1 billion ($1.1 billion), while also fuelling a heated debate over whether Italy’s judiciary is overstepping its role.

title: OpenAI, Anthropic CEOs called to appear at Australian AI probe
full_text:
Investing.com’s stocks of the week
SYDNEY, Sept 27 (Reuters) - The CEOs of OpenAI and Anthropic have been called to appear at an Australian Senate inquiry on AI, the head of the probe said on Sunday, days after the revelation that a rogue OpenAI bot had hacked the country’s health-system database.
The Medicare breach, condemned by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, is one of the highest-profile incidents of AI agents accessing external systems outside the US.
OpenAI’s Sam Altman and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei have been sent written requests to appear at the inquiry, which is to hold public hearings in the capital Canberra on Thursday, said a spokesperson for Senator Sarah Hanson-Young of the Australian Greens party, who chairs the probe.
OpenAI and Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment outside business hours.
The OpenAI agent’s incursion on one of the country’s most used government agencies may prompt Albanese’s Labor government to toughen AI-specific laws it is readying for next year, adding pressure to Australia-US relations already tested by Canberra’s ban on social media for teens, tech policy experts say.
The Senate inquiry is examining the potential impacts of AI and data centres on Australian communities, industries, water and energy. It is one of several state and federal probes into AI.
"There are serious questions for Sam Altman to answer about the OpenAI hack of Australian government websites," Hanson-Young said in a statement. Altman and Amodei "must front up, face the Senate’s questions and have an honest conversation about what effective, lasting regulation of this industry should look like", she said.
Albanese, who revealed the June breach of Medicare on Thursday, called it "unacceptable", saying he had voiced "extreme concern" to Altman.
OpenAI says it only learned of the breach — one of at least four of Australian government websites — in August. It says the incident was not intentional and did not compromise any private information.
